strengths: Large-scale, well-constructed dataset (269M papers, 2,640 subfields, 8,940 tasks) addressing a genuine gap in relation-aware literature retrieval evaluation
Multi-stage quality assurance with transparent construction pipeline (automated computation, rule-based derivation, human validation with 98% LLM-human agreement)
Principled evaluation design grounded in established scientometrics (Uzzi, Funk & Owen-Smith) and collective credit allocation theory
Systematic evaluation across 8 diverse models spanning three paradigms reveals consistent performance patterns and clear limitations of current approaches
Practical validation with downstream literature review application showing 25.3% improvement in survey quality with both automatic and human evaluation
Good reproducibility: implementation details (Faiss indexing), LLM prompts, dataset construction pipeline, and commitment to public release
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging Matthew Effect bias, OCR noise, implicit relationships, and query diversity constraints
weaknesses: Citation-centric ground truth embeds structural biases: conflates citation patterns with scientific merit; may undervalue negative results, niche discoveries, and controversial paradigm-shifting work; Matthew Effect advantage for well-known papers acknowledged but not mitigated

Evaluation metrics may be overly strict (e.g., Recall@50 for novelty/disruption at 1.47%/4.71% penalizes systems that find genuinely novel papers outside top-50; multiple valid citation paths likely exist but alternative paths score zero)

Artificial query generation limits generalization: ego-centric and path-wise queries algorithmically derived, pair-wise queries from citation structure rather than actual user intent; acknowledged lack of linguistic diversity and conversational naturalness

Limited novelty and actionable insights: primarily a benchmarking contribution; results are somewhat expected (current systems lack relational reasoning); only two case studies of 8,940 tasks; no systematic error analysis across subfields or paper types

Incomplete evaluation methodology: only 8 models tested with mixed paradigms (difficult relative comparison); missing baselines (BM25, citation-aware ranking, GNN methods); no ablation studies; closed-box deep research models limit interpretability

Downstream application validation limited: only 40 queries (vs. 8,940 main evaluation); ground truth baseline unfairly has access to true paths; vague system description; missing comparison to existing survey generation systems
Statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests; single run per model; with 8,940 test cases, variance estimates needed

Ground truth arbitrariness in path-wise tasks: BFS with max cumulative citations is reasonable but arbitrary; 'scientific evolution' has multiple valid representations; LLM rationality evaluation introduces circularity via GPT-5 scoring

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of why relation-aware retrieval matters for scientific discovery
Unprecedented dataset scale (269M papers with 2,640 curated subfields) and comprehensive benchmark with 8,940 carefully designed tasks
Novel multi-level task categorization (ego-centric, pair-wise, path-wise) that systematically captures different aspects of relational understanding
Comprehensive evaluation of 8 models across 3 paradigms with multiple complementary metrics showing striking performance gaps
Downstream application demonstrates practical value with 25.3% improvement in literature review quality
Well-organized presentation with detailed appendices, case studies, and honest limitations discussion
Ground truth grounded in established scientometric theory (Uzzi et al., Funk & Owen-Smith)
weaknesses: Critical concern: Ground truth validity questionable across all task types. Ego-centric tasks rely on citation patterns as proxies for novelty/disruptiveness, inheriting well-known Matthew Effect biases. Pair-wise tasks use GPT-5 judgment as ground truth with only 4.8% human validation sample. Path-wise tasks use citation-count-based BFS as ground truth without justifying why this is the uniquely correct scientific evolution path

Evaluation protocol problematic: Recall@50 thresholds lack principled justification—best novelty recall is 1.47%, suggesting either task is fundamentally misspecified or evaluation metric inappropriate. No analysis of whether these thresholds are meaningful for real-world use

Severely limited statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting. Human validation samples extremely small (200/4,200 pair-wise = 4.8%; 50/2,100 path-wise = 2.4%; 40 queries for downstream). Small sample sizes insufficient to support firm conclusions

Downstream application validation inadequate: Only 40 queries evaluated, no inter-annotator agreement statistics reported. Gap between Relation-Augmented and Ground Truth (6.89 vs 8.8) suggests even perfect relation modeling leaves substantial improvement needed

Unfair model comparisons: Embedding models only see title+abstract while other methods may access more information; OpenAI API models accessed differently than self-hosted (potential API instability); no discussion of multiple runs or sensitivity analysis

Query set limitations undermine real-world applicability: Queries are standardized/structured rather than natural user queries (acknowledged in A.4). Paper claims real-world relevance but evaluation uses artificial queries
No solutions or guidance proposed: Paper identifies problems but doesn't suggest how to solve them or provide insights into failure modes beyond high-level case studies

Missing critical analyses: No ablation studies, no quantification of Matthew Effect impact on ground truth, no inter-annotator agreement reported for human validations, GROBID parsing error rates mentioned but not measured
Reproducibility limitations: GPT-5 is proprietary; 'structured rules' for query generation poorly specified; query construction details vague
Limited scope: Only 7 disciplines evaluated; cross-domain generalization unexplored. Main methodology applies established metrics to retrieval rather than proposing novel approaches

strengths: Addresses important gap: First systematic evaluation of relation-aware scientific retrieval with unprecedented scale (269M papers, 2,640 subfields)
Rigorous multi-faceted methodology: Combines objective scientometric indicators, expert human validation (98% agreement on sentiment), and BFS-based path reconstruction grounded in theory
Striking empirical findings: Best models achieve only 1.47% recall on novelty and 4.71% on disruption, clearly demonstrating systematic failures of current retrieval paradigms

Strong reproducibility support: Comprehensive appendices with experimental details (A.2), dataset construction pipeline (A.5), quality assurance (Table 6), LLM prompts (Appendix C), and deployment costs (A.3)
Practical downstream validation: Survey generation experiment shows 25.3% improvement and strong human preference rankings, grounding the benchmark in real applications
Honest limitations discussion: Thorough treatment of Matthew Effect, structural noise, citation network biases, and query standardization issues in Appendix A.4
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with compelling motivation (Figure 1), logical structure, and insightful case studies (Appendix B) illustrating specific failure modes
Distinct contribution: Clearly differentiates from prior benchmarks (LitSearch, PASA, STARK) by focusing on implicit relational reasoning rather than semantic matching or entity extraction
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Primarily a benchmark/dataset paper using established techniques (scientometrics, sentiment classification, BFS); lacks novel methods

Ground truth methodology concerns: (1) Path-wise tasks use BFS with cumulative citation count—a specific choice not fully justified; alternative path criteria could yield different ground truths; (2) Novelty and disruption metrics are time-dependent snapshot computations; temporal stability not analyzed

Inherent bias limitations: Framework privileges highly-cited works and may systematically disadvantage innovative research from underrepresented groups; while Matthew Effect acknowledged, could be more proactive with subfield-specific analysis or alternative metrics
Insufficient downstream validation: Only 40 queries for survey generation; would benefit from larger-scale evaluation across multiple application domains

Pair-wise task performance gaps: Cite-Sentiment and CoMention-Paragraph metrics show very low performance (<18% and <12%), suggesting citation sentiment classification and fine-grained context extraction remain unresolved

Potential embedding model bias: SciBERT pre-trained primarily on biomedical literature; evaluation without domain-specific fine-tuning may unfairly disadvantage embedding methods within their training domain
Query construction lacks linguistic diversity: Queries are primarily standardized test queries from structured rules; real-world queries likely exhibit greater linguistic and conversational variation

Weak impact statement: Brief ethics discussion ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here') given potential fairness implications of ranking systems that privilege established research
Limited inter-annotator validation: 98% agreement on 200 citation sentiments is strong but sample is relatively small; no inter-annotator statistics reported for expert manual verification
